introduction-the-tenancy-dilemma.core: Multi-tenancy options sit on a spectrum: namespaces (cheap, but tenants share the API server, CRDs and cluster-scoped resources) versus separate clusters (strong isolation, but costly and slow to create). Virtual clusters (vCluster) sit in between: each tenant gets its own control plane running inside a namespace of a host cluster.

first_principles.problem: Teams need admin-like freedom (their own CRDs, cluster roles) but separate clusters per team are too expensive.
derivation: **Virtual clusters** for API isolation at low cost.

analogy.title: Rooms in a house versus flats versus separate houses
analogy.story: Rooms share everything, flats have their own front door inside one building, houses are fully separate.
analogy.breaks: Flats have physical walls; virtual clusters still share host nodes unless isolated further.

check.q: What can't namespaces isolate between tenants?
check.a: Cluster-scoped resources like CRDs, ClusterRoles and the shared API server.

architecture-control-planes-inside-contr.core: A vCluster runs as a StatefulSet in a host namespace containing a lightweight Kubernetes API server (often k3s or k8s distro), a data store (SQLite, etcd or external DB), a controller manager and the syncer. Tenants get a kubeconfig to their virtual API, while actual Pods run on the host cluster's nodes.

first_principles.problem: Engineers can't picture how a cluster can live inside another cluster's namespace.
truths: An API server is just a process.
Workloads can be delegated to a host.
derivation: Virtual **API server + store** in a Pod.

analogy.title: A virtual machine for Kubernetes control planes
analogy.story: Like a VM gives you your own OS on shared hardware, vCluster gives you your own cluster API on a shared cluster.
analogy.breaks: VMs virtualise CPUs; vCluster virtualises only the control plane, not nodes.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A full cluster API in seconds.

code.text:
vcluster create team-a --namespace vc-team-a
vcluster connect team-a --namespace vc-team-a
kubectl get namespaces   # team-a's own virtual view

check.q: Where do a virtual cluster's Pods actually run?
check.a: On the host cluster's nodes, synced into the vCluster's host namespace.

the-syncer-the-magic-bridge.core: The syncer watches low-level objects in the virtual cluster (Pods, Services, PVCs, ConfigMaps, Secrets) and creates translated copies in the host namespace with rewritten names, then syncs status back. Higher-level objects (Deployments, CRDs, RBAC) stay virtual-only and are reconciled by the virtual control plane. Sync settings control what crosses the boundary.

first_principles.problem: Tenants create Deployments and CRDs, yet the host cluster only sees renamed Pods in one namespace.
truths: Names must not collide on the host.
Status must flow back to tenants.
derivation: Sync **Pods, Services, PVCs, ConfigMaps, Secrets** down.

analogy.title: A translator between two offices
analogy.story: The client office speaks its own language; the translator files real paperwork with the main office and reports back.
analogy.breaks: Translators summarise; the syncer must map fields precisely or workloads break.

example.title: What the host sees
flow: Host scheduler places them on real nodes
Status synced back to virtual Pods

check.q: Are a tenant's CRDs created in the host cluster?
check.a: No; CRDs and other high-level objects stay in the virtual cluster's own API.

why-use-vcluster-key-use-cases.core: Key use cases: self-service dev environments (each developer or PR gets a cluster in seconds), CI ephemeral clusters for testing operators and CRDs, multi-tenant platforms giving teams admin rights safely, testing Kubernetes version upgrades and isolating SaaS customers' control planes, all at a fraction of dedicated-cluster cost.

first_principles.problem: Every pull request needs a clean cluster to test CRD changes, but provisioning EKS takes 15 minutes and costs money.
truths: Fast, cheap clusters enable new workflows.

analogy.title: Pop-up meeting rooms
analogy.story: Book a fully equipped private room instantly, and return it when done.
analogy.breaks: Meeting rooms are physically separate; vClusters share host nodes and kernels.

example.title: PR pipeline
flow: Install operator + CRDs, run e2e tests

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Clean cluster per PR, almost free.

check.q: Why are vClusters well suited to CI testing of operators?
check.a: They provide an isolated API (own CRDs) in seconds, cheaply, and can be deleted after each run.

vcluster-vs-alternatives-choosing-the-ri.core: Alternatives: plain namespaces with RBAC, quotas and policies (simplest), Hierarchical Namespaces (HNC) for nested policy inheritance, Capsule for tenant objects grouping namespaces, Kamaji or hosted control planes for many real clusters sharing infrastructure, and dedicated clusters for strongest isolation. vCluster wins when tenants need their own API semantics cheaply.

first_principles.problem: A platform team adopts vCluster for everything, including teams that only needed a namespace.
truths: Node isolation is separate from API isolation.
derivation: **Kamaji/hosted control planes** for many real clusters.
**Dedicated clusters + node isolation** for hostile tenants.

analogy.title: Accommodation options
analogy.story: Shared dorm rooms, private rooms, serviced flats or your own house.
analogy.breaks: Accommodation prices are clear; operational costs of tenancy tools are easy to underestimate.

example.title: Decision matrix
flow: Hostile tenants? → dedicated clusters or sandboxed nodes
Many real clusters cheaply? → hosted control planes

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Least complexity that meets the need.

check.q: Does vCluster isolate tenants at the node/kernel level?
check.a: No; it isolates the control plane, while Pods still share host nodes unless you add node-level isolation.
